inputs.need:
I lead the school dental programme for a regional public health unit. Our dental therapists run clinics in 23 primary schools with portable equipment, and since last year they can apply silver diamine fluoride (SDF) to arrest cavities in children who would otherwise wait months for restorative care. Uptake has been disappointing: in the spring term only 41 percent of children with at least one active cavity at the screening visit had SDF applied at the next clinic visit. The therapists say the flow of a clinic day is the problem. Consent forms come back late or not at all, consent for SDF is separate from the general dental consent, children are called from class in an order that suits the timetable rather than treatment need, and the black staining of treated teeth has to be explained to each parent by phone, which takes most of the afternoon.

We want to use lean methods to redesign the SDF pathway: map the value stream from screening to application, find the steps that add waiting and rework, and test changes such as a combined consent form, a call-from-class list ordered by treatment need, and a short photo leaflet about staining. Two things matter to us equally. The first is the numbers: the proportion of children with active cavities who receive SDF soon after screening, and chair time per child. The second is what parents, teachers and therapists make of the changes, especially the staining, which some families find unacceptable on front teeth, and whether children from families who speak little English are being left behind by the consent process.

I need help structuring a lean project that keeps both kinds of evidence without blending them, choosing a primary measure for each strand, and planning structured conversations with parents and staff. We have a data analyst one day a week and the programme's own records, and no research grant.
inputs.constraints: No research grant; a data analyst one day a week. Changes must not add clinic days or therapist hours. Consent materials must be approved by the school board before use. Photographs of children's teeth may not leave the programme's clinical record system.
localFacts: The programme runs dental clinics in 23 primary schools with four dental therapists; each school has a clinic day about every three weeks.
In the spring term, 41 percent of children with at least one active cavity at screening had silver diamine fluoride applied at the next clinic visit.

The public health unit's research ethics committee approved the project on 2026-09-15 as a service evaluation with a research component for the structured conversations (approval PHU-REC-2026-22), with written consent for conversations.
The school board's data-sharing agreement allows the programme to use its own screening and treatment records for evaluation (agreement SB-DSA-2025-09).
A combined consent form has been drafted but not yet approved by the school board.

response.title: Lean redesign of the silver diamine fluoride pathway in a 23-school dental programme
response.subtitle: Lean project with a measurement strand and a conversation strand, reported side by side
response.statement: In a school dental programme serving 23 primary schools, only 41 percent of children with an active cavity at screening received silver diamine fluoride at the next clinic visit last spring. Therapists attribute the gap to the flow of the clinic day: late or missing consent, a separate consent for SDF, children called from class in timetable order, and time spent explaining staining by phone. The project will redesign the pathway with lean methods and judge it by two separate kinds of evidence: timely treatment and chair time, and the views of parents, teachers and therapists, with attention to families who speak little English.
response.whoAffected: Children aged about 5 to 11 with active cavities, their parents, class teachers and school office staff, and four dental therapists.
response.whatHurts: Untreated cavities cause pain, infection and missed school; waiting for consent and searching for children wastes scarce clinic time; staining on front teeth can distress families.
response.currentPractice: Screening visit, separate consent forms sent home in school bags, SDF at a later clinic day if consent returns, children called in timetable order, staining explained by phone.
response.whyNow: SDF is newly available to therapists, uptake is low, and the school board is ready to consider a combined consent form.
response.constraints: No research grant; a data analyst one day a week. Changes must not add clinic days or therapist hours. Consent materials must be approved by the school board before use. Photographs of children's teeth may not leave the programme's clinical record system.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Every child with an active cavity is offered timely, acceptable treatment, and no family is left out because of language or a lost form.
response.summary: Problem framed as a lean redesign of a treatment pathway with two separately measured strands.

records.title: Silver diamine fluoride in school-based dental programmes: caries arrest at six and twelve months
records.authors: Oyelaran-Stroud M, Bergstrom-Achebe T, Rao-Whitfield K
records.abstract: We followed 1,122 children aged 5 to 11 who received silver diamine fluoride for active cavities in a school-based programme. Six months after one application, 72 percent of treated lesions were arrested; among lesions that received a second application at six months, 81 percent were arrested at twelve months. Arrest was lower on lesions that were large and on teeth that were hard to dry in the portable chair. No serious adverse events were recorded. Parents of 6 percent of treated children complained about staining. Children lost to follow-up were more often from schools in deprived areas, so arrest rates may be optimistic.

records.title: Parental acceptability of staining after silver diamine fluoride: choices and conversations
records.abstract: We asked 412 parents of children in school dental programmes to choose between treatment options shown with photographs, and held conversations with 30 of them. Staining after silver diamine fluoride was acceptable to 67 percent of parents on back teeth and to 29 percent on front teeth. Acceptance rose when the alternative was a general anaesthetic or a long wait, and when the photograph showed the stain on a back tooth. Parents wanted to see a photograph before agreeing and resented hearing about the stain only afterwards. Parents who took part in conversations were more often fluent in the majority language than the whole sample.

records.title: Consent return as the bottleneck in school dental programmes: a process mapping study
records.abstract: We mapped the steps from dental screening to treatment in four school dental programmes and timed each step for 600 children. The median time to consent return was 16 days, and 22 percent of consent forms were never returned. Waiting for consent accounted for most of the time between screening and treatment, while chair time was a small share. Forms were lost between school bags, class teachers and the school office. Programmes that sent forms home with a reminder text to parents had faster return. The study did not record the language spoken at home, so it could not say who was least likely to return a form.

records.title: Lean redesign of a school dental clinic day: value stream mapping and chair utilisation
records.authors: Petrakis-Oduya S, Hallberg-Mensah D, Ferreira-Lau N
records.abstract: A school dental team used value stream mapping to redesign its clinic day across eight schools. Changes included a call-from-class list ordered by treatment need, preparation of instruments before children arrived and a single consent check at the door. Chair utilisation rose from 48 percent to 71 percent over two terms, and the number of children treated per clinic day rose from 11 to 16. Therapists reported less time spent waiting for children to be found in class. The evaluation used before-after data without a comparison group, and a new appointment clerk started during the second term.

records.title: Language, consent and treatment in school dental programmes: who is left out?
records.abstract: Using records from a school dental programme serving 31 schools, we linked the language spoken at home to consent return and treatment. Children from families with limited proficiency in the majority language were less likely to have a consent form returned (adjusted odds ratio 0.43) and waited longer for treatment when a form was returned. Translated forms alone made little difference, while a phone call from a bilingual staff member increased return. Children with untreated cavities at the end of the year were concentrated in these families. Home language was missing for 14 percent of children, which may bias the estimates.

records.title: Application time and child cooperation for silver diamine fluoride in mobile school clinics
records.abstract: We timed silver diamine fluoride applications for 214 children in mobile school clinics and recorded cooperation on a simple scale. The median chair time for application was 4 minutes, compared with 22 minutes for a small restoration in the same clinics. Younger children and children who had not visited a dentist before were less cooperative, but most applications were completed at the first attempt. Time spent finding children in class and waiting for them to arrive exceeded chair time on most clinic days. The study was conducted by two experienced therapists, which may limit how far the timings apply to other teams.

records.title: Combined versus separate consent forms for preventive and non-invasive dental treatment in schools
records.abstract: Twelve schools in one programme replaced separate consent forms for examination, fluoride varnish and silver diamine fluoride with a single combined form, while twelve other schools kept separate forms. The combined consent form raised consent return from 58 to 74 percent, while return in schools with separate forms was unchanged. The proportion of parents who ticked the box refusing silver diamine fluoride on the combined form was 11 percent. Schools were not allocated at random, and the combined form included a photograph of staining, so the effects of the two changes cannot be separated.

records.title: Teachers' views of dental clinics in primary schools: disruption, support and responsibility
records.abstract: We held structured conversations with 26 teachers and 9 school office staff in schools that host a dental clinic. Teachers supported the clinics but described disruption when children were called from lessons at unpredictable times, and some said they were left to explain treatment to anxious parents. Office staff were often responsible for chasing consent forms without being told why forms mattered. Participants suggested a timetable agreed in advance and a single point of contact in the dental team. Teachers were recruited through head teachers who favoured the programme, which may have limited critical views.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Waiting for consent, not chair time, dominates the pathway from screening to treatment, and a combined consent form raised return in comparison schools. Lean redesign of the clinic day raised chair utilisation in eight schools. SDF itself arrests most lesions, but staining on front teeth is acceptable to fewer than a third of parents, who want to see a photograph first. Families with limited majority-language proficiency return fewer forms, and bilingual calls help more than translation. Teachers support clinics but want predictable timing. The evidence supports a lean redesign focused on consent and flow, judged separately by numbers and by the views of families and staff.
response.gradeRationale: Before-after reports, non-random comparisons and qualitative studies with selected participants; consistent on where the delays are, imprecise on effect sizes.
response.summary: Eight records appraised; five source-derived claims; certainty low.

response.reading: The value stream runs from screening, through consent, to a clinic day and the call from class. Most of the elapsed time is waiting for consent (c1), and each three-weekly clinic day is a single chance per child. The combined form (c2) and a need-ordered call list (c4) attack waiting and rework; the staining leaflet addresses the reason some parents refuse (c3). Language sits upstream of consent (c5), so a pathway that looks faster on average may leave the same children behind. Teachers and office staff carry parts of the flow without owning it.

response.finer: Both questions are feasible within existing records, one analyst day a week and approved conversations; interesting to the unit and the school board; novel locally; ethical under PHU-REC-2026-22; relevant because uptake is low and some families may be left behind.

response.rationale: The problem is flow and waste in a treatment pathway: most elapsed time is waiting for consent (c1), and lean redesign of the clinic day has raised chair utilisation in the same setting (c4). Value stream mapping finds the waits and rework; test cycles introduce the combined form (c2), the need-ordered call list and the staining leaflet. Two strands are kept apart by design: a measurement strand with its own primary measure, reported by home language (c5), and a conversation strand with its own primary finding on acceptability, including front-tooth staining (c3). They are compared side by side, not merged into one verdict.

response.whyNotMoreComplex: A formal integrated mixed design with joint displays would add analysis time the programme does not have; side-by-side reporting of two pre-specified strands answers the question.

response.overview: Lean project across 23 school clinics, September 2026 to June 2027, in two strands reported side by side. Baseline value stream mapping in four schools, then three test cycles: combined consent form with a staining photograph (once approved), need-ordered call-from-class list, and staining leaflet with a bilingual call for families with limited English. Measurement strand from programme records; conversation strand in six schools.
response.population: Measurement strand: every child screened in the 23 schools during the project. Conversation strand: parents (including parents with limited English, with interpreters), class teachers, office staff and the four therapists in six schools chosen for variation in home language.
response.exposure: The redesigned SDF pathway, introduced change by change.
response.procedures: Value stream mapping session with therapists, a teacher and an office staff member; timing of each step for 60 children in four schools at baseline and after cycle 3. Programme records give screening date, cavities, consent date, home language and SDF date. Structured conversations of 20 to 30 minutes after cycles 1 and 3, recorded with consent and analysed with framework analysis by a researcher not involved in the clinics.

store.protocol.outcomes[0].measure: Proportion of children with at least one active cavity at screening who have silver diamine fluoride applied within 42 days of screening (two clinic visits), from programme records; children absent on both clinic days are reported separately

includes: Lean redesign of the silver diamine fluoride pathway in a 23-school dental programme

response.designSummary: Measurement strand: time series of the 42-day proportion by term and by clinic day across 23 schools, stratified by home language. Conversation strand: framework analysis, reported separately; no statistical integration.
response.sampleSize: About 1,900 children are screened per term and about 520 have an active cavity. The spring figure of 41 percent measured treatment at the next clinic visit, so the baseline for the 42-day window is recomputed from spring 2026 records before cycle 1. If the baseline is near 45 percent and the aim is 60 percent, one term's 520 children estimate the proportion within about plus or minus 4.3 percentage points; each home-language group of about 90 children gives an interval of about plus or minus 10 points, enough to see a gap of 20 points but not a small one. Conversations: about 24 parents (at least 8 with limited English), 8 teachers or office staff and the 4 therapists, reviewed for information power after cycle 1.
response.primaryAnalysis: p-chart of the 42-day proportion by clinic day, limits from the recomputed baseline, with pre-specified rules (one point outside the limits, or eight consecutive points above the centre line); the same chart by home language. Conversation strand: framework analysis with a matrix by group and home language, reported in its own section and then set beside the numbers in a side-by-side table.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Consent return time and never-returned proportion by home language; chair and waiting minutes before and after cycle 3; informed refusals and staining complaints per term.
response.missingData: Children absent on both clinic days in the window are counted in the denominator and reported separately; missing home language (expected about 14 percent) is reported as its own group, not imputed.
response.multiplicity: One primary measure per strand; charts and themes are not subjected to significance tests; secondary measures are descriptive.
response.software: Spreadsheet p-chart templates kept by the analyst; conversation coding in the unit's qualitative software.
overfittingGuards: Window, denominator and chart rules fixed before cycle 1, after the investigator's edit
No merged score combining the two strands
Themes developed before the analyst shares the charts with the conversation researcher
response.summary: Analysis for the 42-day measure with a recomputed baseline, by home language, and a separate conversation strand.

store.protocol.outcomes[0].measure: Proportion of children with at least one active cavity at screening who have silver diamine fluoride applied within 42 days of screening (two clinic visits), from programme records; children absent on both clinic days are reported separately

response.risks: Low: the pathway changes are service changes; conversations carry the risk of parents feeling judged about their child's teeth or their English, and of teachers feeling blamed for disruption.
response.consent: The redesigned combined consent form is the clinical consent for treatment; the evaluation uses programme records under agreement SB-DSA-2025-09 without individual consent. Structured conversations need written consent (PHU-REC-2026-22), with interpreters and translated information for parents with limited English.
response.data: Records are analysed inside the programme's systems with study numbers; photographs of teeth never leave the clinical record system; conversation recordings are deleted after transcription.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: home language, deprivation of the school catchment and family structure shape consent return and acceptability. The primary measure is reported by home language, families with limited English are purposively invited to conversations with interpreters, and the bilingual call is part of the change package.
response.effectiveness: Success means more children treated soon after screening in every language group, with acceptable staining decisions made by families; either strand failing is reported as such.
response.efficiency: No added clinic days; the analyst's day a week covers the measurement strand.
response.costs: Printing of forms and leaflets, interpreter time for conversations; within the programme budget.
response.partnerships: The school board, two head teachers, a parents' group from a school with many families who speak little English, and the four therapists.
response.rebPath: Approved by the public health unit's research ethics committee on 2026-09-15 as a service evaluation with a research component (PHU-REC-2026-22); the combined form still needs school board approval before cycle 1.
response.limitations: Uncontrolled time series; conversation sample limited to six schools; seasonal changes in attendance.
response.summary: Low-risk project with written consent for conversations, interpreters, and results by home language.

response.partnershipPlan: A parents' group from a school where many families speak little English reviews the combined form and the staining leaflet; a teacher and an office staff member join the value stream mapping session; the therapists review every change before it is tested.
response.socialListening: The programme's parent feedback line and school newsletters are reviewed for comments about the clinics; no social media listening.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase: If I had seen the picture I would have said yes for the back teeth and no for the front one.
items.implication: Put the staining photograph on the combined form and allow tooth-by-tooth choices.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase (through an interpreter): The letter came home but nobody in the house could read it, so it stayed in the bag.
items.implication: Bilingual phone call as part of the change package.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase (teacher): I never know when they will come for a child; it is usually in the middle of reading.
items.implication: Agree a call timetable with each school.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase (dental therapist): I spend longer explaining the stain on the phone than applying it in the chair.
items.implication: Leaflet and form do the explaining; calls kept for questions.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase (school office): Nobody told us why the pink form mattered more than the others.
items.implication: Brief office staff on the pathway and give them one contact.

response.summary: Five composite voices on staining, language, class disruption, therapist time and office work.

response.title: Lean redesign of a silver diamine fluoride pathway in 23 school dental clinics: timely treatment and acceptability reported side by side
response.abstract: Problem: only 41 percent of children with an active cavity received silver diamine fluoride at the next school clinic visit. Intervention: lean redesign with a combined consent form and staining photograph, a need-ordered call list, a staining leaflet and bilingual calls. Measures: the proportion treated within 42 days of screening by home language (measurement strand) and the acceptability of the pathway to parents, teachers and therapists (conversation strand), reported side by side. Results will follow the project.
response.introduction: Silver diamine fluoride arrests most cavities, but school programmes lose time waiting for consent, and staining on front teeth is unacceptable to many parents. Families with limited majority-language proficiency return fewer consent forms.
response.methods: Value stream mapping, three test cycles, programme records analysed as p-charts by home language, and structured conversations analysed with framework analysis; ethics approval PHU-REC-2026-22.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present the two strands in separate sections and a side-by-side table.
response.discussion: The discussion will ask whether the two strands agree, what informed refusals mean for the measure, and whether any language group was left behind.
response.limitations: Uncontrolled time series; six-school conversation sample; baseline for the 42-day window recomputed from records.
response.conclusion: To be written after the project, strand by strand.
response.reportingChecklist: SQUIRE 2.0, with COREQ items for the conversation strand
response.summary: Draft with two strands kept separate and results left empty.
